## Introduction

This project investigates the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI), automation risk, industry, and required education.
The analysis focuses on three main questions:

1. Which industries have the greatest share of jobs with High AI impact?
2. Is AI impact level related to automation risk across different industries?
3. Is higher required education associated with lower automation risk?

## Data Preparation

### Loading Packages and Data

```{r load}
library(tidyverse)   # includes ggplot2 and dplyr

jobs <- read.csv(
  "ai_job_trends_dataset.csv",
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

### Initial Data Exploration

We first examine the dimensions, variable types, missing values, and duplicate observations in the dataset.

```{r explore}
dim(jobs)
str(jobs)
colSums(is.na(jobs))
sum(duplicated(jobs))
```

### Renaming and Organizing Variables

We rename the variables used in our analysis to make the code easier to read. We also organize AI impact and education into ordered categorical factors.

```{r rename}
jobs <- jobs %>%
  rename(
    job_title        = `Job Title`,
    job_status       = `Job Status`,
    location         = Location,
    industry         = Industry,
    ai_impact        = `AI Impact Level`,
    education        = `Required Education`,
    automation_risk  = `Automation Risk (%)`,
    salary           = `Median Salary (USD)`,
    experience       = `Experience Required (Years)`,
    openings_2024    = `Job Openings (2024)`,
    openings_2030    = `Projected Openings (2030)`,
    remote_ratio     = `Remote Work Ratio (%)`,
    gender_diversity = `Gender Diversity (%)`
  )

jobs <- jobs %>%
  mutate(
    ai_impact = factor(
      ai_impact,
      levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(
        "High School",
        "Associate Degree",
        "Bachelor’s Degree",
        "Master’s Degree",
        "PhD"
      )
    )
  )

table(jobs$ai_impact, useNA = "ifany")
table(jobs$education, useNA = "ifany")
```

### Numeric Scores for Correlation

A correlation needs numbers, so we convert the ordered categories into scores
(AI impact: Low = 1, Moderate = 2, High = 3; education: High School = 1 ... PhD = 5).
Because these are ranks rather than true measurements, we use **Spearman's rank correlation (ρ)**,
which only assumes the categories are in the right order.

```{r scores}
jobs <- jobs %>%
  mutate(
    ai_score        = as.integer(ai_impact),
    edu_score       = as.integer(education),
    openings_growth = (openings_2030 - openings_2024) / openings_2024 * 100,
    log_growth      = log(openings_2030 / openings_2024)  # symmetric growth measure for regression
  )

# Spearman correlation with p-value and an approximate 95% confidence interval
# (Fisher z-transformation). Returns a one-row tibble so it can be used in summarise().
spearman_ci <- function(x, y) {
  ok  <- complete.cases(x, y)
  n   <- sum(ok)
  rho <- cor(x[ok], y[ok], method = "spearman")
  se  <- 1 / sqrt(n - 3)
  p   <- cor.test(x[ok], y[ok], method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  tibble(
    n       = n,
    rho     = rho,
    lower   = tanh(atanh(rho) - 1.96 * se),
    upper   = tanh(atanh(rho) + 1.96 * se),
    p_value = p
  )
}

# Short label used in plot subtitles
cor_label <- function(res) {
  sprintf("Spearman ρ = %.3f  [95%% CI %.3f to %.3f],  p = %.3f,  n = %s",
          res$rho, res$lower, res$upper, res$p_value,
          format(res$n, big.mark = ","))
}
```

## Overview: Correlation Matrix

### Graph 1: Correlations Between All Numeric Variables

Before answering the individual questions, this heatmap shows the Spearman correlation between every pair
of numeric variables. Values near +1 or −1 are strong relationships; values near 0 mean no relationship.

```{r graph1, fig.height = 6.5}
num_vars <- jobs %>%
  transmute(
    `AI impact (1-3)`  = ai_score,
    `Education (1-5)`  = edu_score,
    `Automation risk`  = automation_risk,
    `Salary`           = salary,
    `Experience`       = experience,
    `Remote ratio`     = remote_ratio,
    `Openings growth`  = openings_growth,
    `Gender diversity` = gender_diversity
  )

cor_mat <- cor(num_vars, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat)) %>%
  rename(var1 = Var1, var2 = Var2, rho = Freq)

plot1 <- ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = rho)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", rho)), size = 3.3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2A9D8F", mid = "white", high = "#E76F51",
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(
    title    = "Spearman Correlation Matrix",
    subtitle = "Every off-diagonal value is close to 0",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "ρ"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank())

plot1
```

## Question 1: Which industries have the greatest share of High AI impact?

We calculate the percentage of records classified as High AI impact within each industry, and the
average automation risk in that industry, so that we can also see whether industries with more High AI
impact jobs carry more automation risk.

### Summary Table

```{r q1_table}
industry_summary <- jobs %>%
  group_by(industry) %>%
  summarise(
    records             = n(),
    high_impact_records = sum(ai_impact == "High", na.rm = TRUE),
    high_impact_percent = mean(ai_impact == "High", na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    mean_risk           = mean(automation_risk, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(high_impact_percent))

industry_summary

industry_cor <- cor.test(industry_summary$high_impact_percent,
                         industry_summary$mean_risk)
industry_cor
```

### Graph 2: Share of High AI Impact vs Average Automation Risk (Industry Level)

Each point is one industry. The x-axis answers Question 1 (further right = larger share of High AI impact);
the y-axis shows whether those industries also have higher average automation risk.
Note the axes are zoomed in: all industries fall within a few percentage points of each other.

```{r graph2}
plot2 <- ggplot(industry_summary, aes(x = high_impact_percent, y = mean_risk)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "grey40", fill = "grey85") +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, color = "#E76F51") +
  geom_text(aes(label = industry), vjust = -1, size = 3.4) +
  labs(
    title    = "Industries: Share of High AI Impact vs Average Automation Risk",
    subtitle = sprintf("Pearson r = %.2f, p = %.2f (only 8 industries, so treat with caution)",
                       industry_cor$estimate, industry_cor$p.value),
    x = "Records classified as High AI impact (%)",
    y = "Average automation risk (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot2
```

## Question 2: Is AI impact level related to automation risk across different industries?

### Overall Correlation

```{r q2_overall}
ai_cor_overall <- spearman_ci(jobs$ai_score, jobs$automation_risk)
ai_cor_overall

impact_risk_summary <- jobs %>%
  group_by(ai_impact, ai_score) %>%
  summarise(
    records     = n(),
    mean_risk   = mean(automation_risk, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_risk = median(automation_risk, na.rm = TRUE),
    se          = sd(automation_risk, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

impact_risk_summary
```

### Graph 3: Scatter Plot of AI Impact vs Automation Risk

Each grey dot is one job record (jittered sideways so the 30,000 points don't stack on top of each other).
The black points are group means with 95% confidence intervals, and the orange line is the linear trend.
A real relationship would show the line clearly sloping up or down.

```{r graph3}
plot3 <- ggplot(jobs, aes(x = ai_score, y = automation_risk)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.3, height = 0, alpha = 0.05, size = 0.6, color = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "#E76F51", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_pointrange(
    data = impact_risk_summary,
    aes(y = mean_risk, ymin = mean_risk - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean_risk + 1.96 * se),
    color = "black", size = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3, labels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title    = "AI Impact Level vs Automation Risk",
    subtitle = cor_label(ai_cor_overall),
    x = "AI impact level",
    y = "Automation risk (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot3
```

ai_cor_by_industry

## Question 3: Is higher required education associated with lower automation risk?

It is important to note that the dataset measures the education required for a job, not the actual educational attainment of individual workers.

If higher education protected against automation, we would expect a **negative** correlation.

### Summary Table

```{r q3_table}
edu_cor_overall <- spearman_ci(jobs$edu_score, jobs$automation_risk)
edu_cor_overall

education_summary <- jobs %>%
  group_by(education, edu_score) %>%
  summarise(
    records     = n(),
    mean_risk   = mean(automation_risk, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_risk = median(automation_risk, na.rm = TRUE),
    se          = sd(automation_risk, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

education_summary
```

### Graph 5: Scatter Plot of Required Education vs Automation Risk

```{r graph5}
plot5 <- ggplot(jobs, aes(x = edu_score, y = automation_risk)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.3, height = 0, alpha = 0.05, size = 0.6, color = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "#2A9D8F", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_pointrange(
    data = education_summary,
    aes(y = mean_risk, ymin = mean_risk - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean_risk + 1.96 * se),
    color = "black", size = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 1:5,
    labels = c("High School", "Associate", "Bachelor's", "Master's", "PhD")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Required Education vs Automation Risk",
    subtitle = cor_label(edu_cor_overall),
    x = "Required education",
    y = "Automation risk (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot5
```

### Graph 6: Correlation Strength by Industry (AI Impact and Education)

This chart summarises Questions 2 and 3 together. Each point is the Spearman correlation between the
predictor and automation risk within one industry, with its 95% confidence interval.
The shaded band (−0.1 to 0.1) is the conventional range for a *negligible* correlation.
Intervals that cross the dashed zero line are not statistically significant.

```{r graph6, fig.height = 6}
industry_levels <- c("All industries", sort(unique(jobs$industry)))

forest_data <- bind_rows(
  ai_cor_by_industry %>%
    mutate(predictor = "AI impact level"),
  ai_cor_overall %>%
    mutate(industry = "All industries", predictor = "AI impact level"),
  jobs %>%
    group_by(industry) %>%
    summarise(spearman_ci(edu_score, automation_risk), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(predictor = "Required education"),
  edu_cor_overall %>%
    mutate(industry = "All industries", predictor = "Required education")
) %>%
  mutate(
    industry = factor(industry, levels = rev(industry_levels)),
    overall  = industry == "All industries"
  )

plot6 <- ggplot(forest_data, aes(x = rho, y = industry, color = predictor)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.1, xmax = 0.1, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey90", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper, shape = overall), size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ predictor) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("AI impact level" = "#E76F51",
                                "Required education" = "#2A9D8F")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 16, `TRUE` = 18)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.15, 0.15)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Correlation with Automation Risk, by Industry",
    subtitle = "Spearman ρ with 95% CI; grey band = negligible (|ρ| < 0.1)",
    x = "Spearman ρ with automation risk",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

plot6
```


# Part 2: Which Factors Matter? Screening Every Relationship

So far we tested the three relationships we expected. Here we test **every pair of variables** to find
any factor that might be related to automation risk (or to anything else). Each pair gets the test that
fits its variable types:

| Pair type | Test | Strength measure (0 = none, 1 = perfect) |
|---|---|---|
| numeric – numeric | Spearman correlation | \|ρ\| |
| category – numeric | one-way ANOVA | η (square root of R²) |
| category – category | chi-squared test | Cramér's V |

When we run many tests, some will be "significant" by chance alone: at p < 0.05 about 1 in 20 tests
is a false positive. We therefore also apply the **Bonferroni correction** (multiply each p-value by the
number of tests) and the **Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate**.

```{r screening}
assoc_test <- function(x, y) {
  x_cat <- !is.numeric(x)
  y_cat <- !is.numeric(y)

  if (!x_cat && !y_cat) {
    ct <- cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
    tibble(method = "Spearman |ρ|", strength = abs(unname(ct$estimate)), p_value = ct$p.value)
  } else if (x_cat && y_cat) {
    tab <- table(x, y)
    ch  <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))
    v   <- sqrt(unname(ch$statistic) / (sum(tab) * (min(dim(tab)) - 1)))
    tibble(method = "Cramér's V", strength = v, p_value = ch$p.value)
  } else {
    num <- if (x_cat) y else x
    grp <- if (x_cat) x else y
    fit <- lm(num ~ grp)
    tibble(method = "η (ANOVA)", strength = sqrt(summary(fit)$r.squared),
           p_value = anova(fit)$`Pr(>F)`[1])
  }
}

screen_vars <- jobs %>%
  select(automation_risk, ai_score, edu_score, salary, experience, remote_ratio,
         gender_diversity, openings_2024, openings_2030, openings_growth,
         industry, location, job_status)

var_pairs <- combn(names(screen_vars), 2, simplify = FALSE)

screening <- map_dfr(var_pairs, function(p) {
  assoc_test(screen_vars[[p[1]]], screen_vars[[p[2]]]) %>%
    mutate(var1 = p[1], var2 = p[2], .before = 1)
}) %>%
  mutate(
    p_bonferroni = p.adjust(p_value, method = "bonferroni"),
    p_fdr        = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"),
    # openings_growth is calculated from the two openings columns, so those pairs are built-in
    mechanical   = var2 == "openings_growth" & var1 %in% c("openings_2024", "openings_2030")
  ) %>%
  arrange(p_value)

nrow(screening)                                   # number of tests run
sum(screening$p_value < 0.05)                     # "significant" before correction
nrow(screening) * 0.05                            # how many we'd expect by chance alone
sum(screening$p_bonferroni < 0.05 & !screening$mechanical)  # real findings after correction

screening %>% head(10)
```

### Graph 7: Association Strength Between All Variables

Unlike Graph 1, this matrix also includes the categorical variables (industry, location, job status),
so every factor in the dataset is compared with every other one on the same 0–1 scale.

```{r graph7, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 10}
var_order <- names(screen_vars)

assoc_matrix <- bind_rows(
  screening %>% select(var1, var2, strength),
  screening %>% select(var1 = var2, var2 = var1, strength)
) %>%
  mutate(
    var1 = factor(var1, levels = var_order),
    var2 = factor(var2, levels = var_order)
  )

plot7 <- ggplot(assoc_matrix, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = strength)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", strength)), size = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#D94801", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(
    title    = "Association Strength Between Every Pair of Variables",
    subtitle = "|ρ|, η or Cramér's V depending on variable types. Only the openings/growth cells are non-zero, and those are calculated from each other",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Strength"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank())

plot7
```

### Graph 8: Which Relationships Are Statistically Significant?

Each bar is one of the variable pairs, ranked by evidence (taller = smaller p-value). Bars past the
dashed line are significant at p < 0.05 *on their own*; bars past the solid line remain significant after
correcting for the number of tests.

```{r graph8, fig.height = 11}
n_tests <- nrow(screening)

screen_plot_data <- screening %>%
  mutate(
    pair     = paste(var1, "×", var2),
    log_p    = pmin(-log10(pmax(p_value, 1e-16)), 16),   # cap p = 0 at 1e-16 so it can be drawn
    category = case_when(
      mechanical                  ~ "Built-in (calculated from each other)",
      p_bonferroni < 0.05         ~ "Significant after correction",
      p_value < 0.05              ~ "p < 0.05 only (likely chance)",
      TRUE                        ~ "Not significant"
    )
  )

plot8 <- ggplot(screen_plot_data, aes(x = reorder(pair, log_p), y = log_p, fill = category)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05 / n_tests)) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 6)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Built-in (calculated from each other)" = "grey60",
    "Significant after correction"          = "#D94801",
    "p < 0.05 only (likely chance)"         = "#E9C46A",
    "Not significant"                       = "#2A9D8F"
  )) +
  labs(
    title    = "Significance Screening of All Variable Pairs",
    subtitle = sprintf("Dashed line: p = 0.05.  Solid line: Bonferroni threshold p = 0.05 / %d", n_tests),
    x = NULL, y = "-log10(p-value)  (larger = stronger evidence)", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))

plot8
```

### Graph 9: Scatter Plot Matrix of the Continuous Variables

A random sample of 1,500 jobs, plotting every continuous variable against every other one, with a linear
trend line and the correlation in each panel. Real relationships show up as tilted clouds; here every
cloud is a flat, evenly filled rectangle.

```{r graph9, fig.height = 10, fig.width = 10}
sm_vars <- jobs %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1500) %>%
  transmute(
    `Automation risk`   = automation_risk,
    `Salary ($k)`       = salary / 1000,
    `Experience (yrs)`  = experience,
    `Remote %`          = remote_ratio,
    `Gender div. %`     = gender_diversity,
    `Log growth`        = log_growth
  ) %>%
  mutate(id = row_number())

sm_levels <- setdiff(names(sm_vars), "id")

sm_long <- sm_vars %>%
  pivot_longer(-id, names_to = "x_var", values_to = "x") %>%
  inner_join(
    sm_vars %>% pivot_longer(-id, names_to = "y_var", values_to = "y"),
    by = "id"
  ) %>%
  filter(x_var != y_var) %>%
  mutate(
    x_var = factor(x_var, levels = sm_levels),
    y_var = factor(y_var, levels = sm_levels)
  )

sm_labels <- sm_long %>%
  group_by(x_var, y_var) %>%
  summarise(r = cor(x, y, method = "spearman"), .groups = "drop")

plot9 <- ggplot(sm_long, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.4, color = "grey30") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#E76F51", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_label(
    data = sm_labels,
    aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = sprintf("ρ = %.2f", r)),
    hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.2, size = 2.6, label.size = 0, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_grid(y_var ~ x_var, scales = "free", switch = "both") +
  labs(title = "Scatter Plot Matrix (random sample of 1,500 jobs)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.placement = "outside",
    strip.text      = element_text(size = 8),
    axis.text       = element_text(size = 6)
  )

plot9
```

### Graph 10: Does AI Impact Change How Salary Relates to Automation Risk?

A common hypothesis is that well-paid jobs are safer from automation, and that this protection is weaker
when AI impact is high. If so, the three trend lines would slope downward and differ from each other.

```{r graph10}
plot10 <- ggplot(jobs, aes(x = salary / 1000, y = automation_risk, color = ai_impact)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.04, size = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Low" = "#2A9D8F", "Moderate" = "#E9C46A", "High" = "#E76F51")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Salary vs Automation Risk by AI Impact Level",
    subtitle = sprintf("Overall Spearman ρ = %.3f", cor(jobs$salary, jobs$automation_risk, method = "spearman")),
    x = "Median salary (USD, thousands)",
    y = "Automation risk (%)",
    color = "AI impact"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1)))

plot10
```

### Graph 11: Job-Title Level — Share of High AI Impact vs Average Risk

The same job title appears many times (639 titles, about 47 records each). If AI impact were a property of
the job itself, titles with more High AI impact records should have higher average risk.

```{r graph11}
title_summary <- jobs %>%
  group_by(job_title) %>%
  summarise(
    records             = n(),
    high_impact_percent = mean(ai_impact == "High") * 100,
    mean_risk           = mean(automation_risk),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

title_cor <- cor.test(title_summary$high_impact_percent, title_summary$mean_risk,
                      method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)

# Does job title explain automation risk at all? (one-way ANOVA across 639 titles)
title_anova <- anova(lm(automation_risk ~ job_title, data = jobs))
title_anova

plot11 <- ggplot(title_summary, aes(x = high_impact_percent, y = mean_risk)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = records), alpha = 0.5, color = "#264653") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "#E76F51") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.8, 3)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Job Titles: Share of High AI Impact vs Average Automation Risk",
    subtitle = sprintf("Spearman ρ = %.3f, p = %.3f (n = %d titles). Job title ANOVA p = %.2f",
                       title_cor$estimate, title_cor$p.value, nrow(title_summary),
                       title_anova$`Pr(>F)`[1]),
    x = "Records of this title classified as High AI impact (%)",
    y = "Average automation risk (%)",
    size = "Records"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot11
```

## Data Quality Checks

Before building regression models it is worth checking that the variables mean what their names say.

### Graph 12: Does "Job Status" Match the Change in Openings?

A job labelled "Increasing" should have more openings in 2030 than in 2024 (above the diagonal line).

```{r graph12}
status_check <- jobs %>%
  group_by(job_status) %>%
  summarise(
    records             = n(),
    pct_openings_rising = mean(openings_2030 > openings_2024) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

status_check

plot12 <- ggplot(jobs, aes(x = openings_2024, y = openings_2030)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.4, color = "#264653") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#E76F51", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_label(
    data = status_check,
    aes(x = 2500, y = 9700, label = sprintf("%.1f%% above the line", pct_openings_rising)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ job_status) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title    = "Job Openings 2024 vs Projected 2030, by Job Status Label",
    subtitle = "Red line = no change. The label does not predict whether openings rise",
    x = "Openings (2024)", y = "Projected openings (2030)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot12
```

### Graph 13: Distribution of Automation Risk

```{r graph13}
ks_risk <- suppressWarnings(ks.test(jobs$automation_risk, "punif", min = 0, max = 100))
ks_risk

plot13 <- ggplot(jobs, aes(x = automation_risk)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2.5, boundary = 0, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = nrow(jobs) / 40, linetype = "dashed", color = "#E76F51", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of Automation Risk",
    subtitle = sprintf("Dashed line = perfectly uniform distribution. Kolmogorov–Smirnov test vs uniform: p = %.2f",
                       ks_risk$p.value),
    x = "Automation risk (%)", y = "Number of records"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot13
```

A flat histogram and a non-significant test mean we cannot distinguish automation risk from a random
number drawn evenly between 0 and 100.

# Part 3: Regression Analysis

Correlations look at one factor at a time. Multiple regression estimates the effect of **each factor while
holding all the others constant**, which is the closest we can get to isolating a factor's own impact in
observational data.

**Model 1 (main):** automation risk explained by AI impact, education, industry, location, job status,
salary, experience, remote ratio and gender diversity.
Continuous predictors are standardised (z-scores), so their coefficients mean
"change in automation risk (percentage points) for a one standard deviation increase".
Categorical coefficients are differences from the reference group
(Low AI impact, High School, Education industry, Australia, Decreasing status).

```{r model_prep}
jobs_model <- jobs %>%
  mutate(
    industry   = factor(industry),
    location   = factor(location),
    job_status = factor(job_status),
    across(
      c(salary, experience, remote_ratio, gender_diversity, automation_risk),
      ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)),
      .names = "{.col}_z"
    )
  )
```

### Model 1: Automation Risk

```{r model1}
risk_model <- lm(
  automation_risk ~ ai_impact + education + industry + location + job_status +
    salary_z + experience_z + remote_ratio_z + gender_diversity_z,
  data = jobs_model
)

summary(risk_model)

# F-test for each factor as a whole (e.g. all 7 industry dummies together)
drop1(risk_model, test = "F")
```

### Interaction Tests: Does the Effect of AI Impact Depend on Industry or Education?

An interaction asks whether the effect of AI impact is different in different industries. We compare a
model without the interaction to one with it using an F-test.

```{r interactions}
m_ai_ind     <- lm(automation_risk ~ ai_impact + industry, data = jobs_model)
m_ai_ind_int <- lm(automation_risk ~ ai_impact * industry, data = jobs_model)

m_ai_edu     <- lm(automation_risk ~ ai_impact + education, data = jobs_model)
m_ai_edu_int <- lm(automation_risk ~ ai_impact * education, data = jobs_model)

m_sal_ai     <- lm(automation_risk ~ ai_impact + salary_z, data = jobs_model)
m_sal_ai_int <- lm(automation_risk ~ ai_impact * salary_z, data = jobs_model)

interaction_tests <- tibble(
  interaction = c("AI impact × industry", "AI impact × education", "AI impact × salary"),
  p_value = c(
    anova(m_ai_ind, m_ai_ind_int)$`Pr(>F)`[2],
    anova(m_ai_edu, m_ai_edu_int)$`Pr(>F)`[2],
    anova(m_sal_ai, m_sal_ai_int)$`Pr(>F)`[2]
  )
)

interaction_tests
```

### Graph 14: Regression Coefficients With 95% Confidence Intervals

Each point is the estimated effect of a factor on automation risk, holding the others constant.
A factor matters if its confidence interval stays clear of the zero line.

```{r graph14, fig.height = 8}
coef_data <- broom::tidy(risk_model, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    group = case_when(
      str_starts(term, "ai_impact")  ~ "AI impact (vs Low)",
      str_starts(term, "education")  ~ "Education (vs High School)",
      str_starts(term, "industry")   ~ "Industry (vs Education)",
      str_starts(term, "location")   ~ "Location (vs Australia)",
      str_starts(term, "job_status") ~ "Job status",
      TRUE                           ~ "Continuous (per 1 SD)"
    ),
    label = term %>%
      str_remove("^(ai_impact|education|industry|location|job_status)") %>%
      str_replace("_z$", "") %>%
      str_replace_all("_", " "),
    significant = p.value < 0.05
  )

plot14 <- ggplot(coef_data, aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(label, estimate), color = significant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  facet_grid(group ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey50", `TRUE` = "#D94801"),
                     labels = c(`FALSE` = "Not significant", `TRUE` = "p < 0.05")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Effect of Each Factor on Automation Risk (Multiple Regression)",
    subtitle = sprintf("R² = %.4f, adjusted R² = %.4f, overall F-test p = %.2f",
                       summary(risk_model)$r.squared, summary(risk_model)$adj.r.squared,
                       pf(summary(risk_model)$fstatistic[1], summary(risk_model)$fstatistic[2],
                          summary(risk_model)$fstatistic[3], lower.tail = FALSE)),
    x = "Change in automation risk (percentage points)", y = NULL, color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0), legend.position = "bottom")

plot14
```

### Model 2: Projected Job Growth

As a second outcome we model job growth between 2024 and 2030 (log of the ratio, so a doubling and a
halving are equally large in opposite directions), including automation risk as a predictor.
If automation risk had real consequences, high-risk jobs should be projected to shrink.

```{r model2}
growth_model <- lm(
  log_growth ~ automation_risk_z + ai_impact + education + industry + location +
    salary_z + experience_z + remote_ratio_z + gender_diversity_z,
  data = jobs_model
)

summary(growth_model)
drop1(growth_model, test = "F")
```

### Graph 15: How Much Does Each Factor Explain?

Partial η² is the share of the remaining variation in the outcome that a factor explains on its own,
after the other factors are accounted for. 0.01 is conventionally a "small" effect, 0.06 "medium" and
0.14 "large". The x-axis is zoomed in far below even a small effect.

```{r graph15, fig.height = 6}
term_importance <- function(model, outcome) {
  drop1(model, test = "F") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column("term") %>%
    filter(term != "<none>") %>%
    transmute(
      outcome,
      term = str_replace(term, "_z$", "") %>% str_replace_all("_", " "),
      partial_eta2 = `Sum of Sq` / (`Sum of Sq` + deviance(model)),
      p_value = `Pr(>F)`
    )
}

importance <- bind_rows(
  term_importance(risk_model,   "Outcome: automation risk"),
  term_importance(growth_model, "Outcome: log job growth")
)

importance

plot15 <- ggplot(importance,
                 aes(x = partial_eta2, y = reorder(term, partial_eta2), fill = p_value < 0.05)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("p = %.2f", p_value)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.002), labels = function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#2A9D8F", `TRUE` = "#D94801"),
                    labels = c(`FALSE` = "Not significant", `TRUE` = "p < 0.05")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Variance Explained by Each Factor (Partial η²)",
    subtitle = "A 'small' effect would be 0.01, five times beyond the right edge of this axis",
    x = "Partial η²", y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

plot15
```

### Graph 16: Can the Model Predict Automation Risk for New Jobs?

The strictest test of a model is to fit it on 70% of the data and predict the other 30%. A useful model
puts the points near the red diagonal; a useless one predicts roughly the average for everyone.

```{r graph16}
train_idx  <- sample(nrow(jobs_model), size = round(0.7 * nrow(jobs_model)))
train_data <- jobs_model[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- jobs_model[-train_idx, ]

risk_model_train <- update(risk_model, data = train_data)
test_data$predicted <- predict(risk_model_train, newdata = test_data)

test_r2 <- 1 - sum((test_data$automation_risk - test_data$predicted)^2) /
               sum((test_data$automation_risk - mean(train_data$automation_risk))^2)
test_rmse <- sqrt(mean((test_data$automation_risk - test_data$predicted)^2))

c(test_r2 = test_r2, test_rmse = test_rmse)

plot16 <- ggplot(test_data, aes(x = predicted, y = automation_risk)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.6, color = "#264653") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#E76F51", linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Predicted vs Actual Automation Risk (30% Hold-Out Data)",
    subtitle = sprintf("Out-of-sample R² = %.4f, RMSE = %.1f points. Predictions are all squeezed near 50%%",
                       test_r2, test_rmse),
    x = "Predicted automation risk (%)", y = "Actual automation risk (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot16
```

# Part 4: Correlation vs Causality

A regression coefficient is not proof that one factor *causes* a change in another. To argue causality
from observational data we would need, at minimum:

1. **An association** that is strong and consistent across subgroups.
2. **Correct time ordering**: the cause measured before the effect. This dataset is a single snapshot,
   so we cannot tell which came first.
3. **No unmeasured confounders**: other factors that drive both variables. We controlled for the
   variables available (Model 1), but variables such as task routineness or firm size are absent.
4. **A plausible mechanism** and, ideally, a natural experiment or randomised comparison.

In this dataset the first condition already fails: there is no association to explain, either before or
after controlling for other factors. So the data supports **no causal claim in either direction**:
not that AI impact raises automation risk, and not that education protects against it.

# Conclusion

**Question 1.** Every industry has close to one third of its records classified as High AI impact
(32.6% in Education to 33.9% in Finance), so industry differences in AI impact are small. With only
eight industries, the industry-level correlation in Graph 2 is not reliable evidence either way.

**Question 2.** AI impact level is essentially unrelated to automation risk. The overall Spearman
correlation is about ρ = 0.01 and is not statistically significant at the 5% level; average risk is
roughly 50% for Low, Moderate and High alike. Within individual industries the correlations all fall in
the negligible band (Graph 6), and the AI impact × industry interaction is not significant, so the
(absent) relationship does not differ between industries.

**Question 3.** Required education is also not associated with lower automation risk (ρ ≈ 0.01, not
significant). Jobs requiring a PhD have about the same average risk as jobs requiring a high school
diploma, in every industry.

**Which factors matter?** We screened all 78 variable pairs. Five reached p < 0.05 on their own, about what
chance alone would produce (78 × 0.05 ≈ 4). None survived the Bonferroni correction except the pairs where
one variable is calculated from the other. Job title, salary, experience, location, remote ratio and
gender diversity are all unrelated to automation risk.

**Regression.** The multiple regression of automation risk on all nine factors explains less than 0.1% of
the variation (R² ≈ 0.0007), its overall F-test is not significant, and on held-out data it predicts no
better than simply guessing the average (out-of-sample R² ≈ 0). The model of projected job growth is
equally flat: automation risk does not predict whether a job is expected to grow or shrink.

**Interpretation.** The data quality checks explain why. Automation risk is statistically
indistinguishable from a uniform random number between 0 and 100 (Graph 13), and the "Job Status" label
matches the actual direction of change in openings only about 50% of the time, no better than a coin flip
(Graph 12). This strongly suggests the dataset is synthetic, with each column generated independently.
The correct conclusion is therefore that **this dataset contains no relationships between AI impact,
automation risk, industry and education**, not that no such relationships exist in the real labour market.
Answering those questions would require data in which automation risk is measured from real job tasks.
